content: The timing of sessions should be convenient, and organizers and facilitators must be skilled in encouraging active participation from everyone involved. Gender-related indicators are essential for monitoring acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) detection systems. These include calculating the percentage of AFP cases by sex with final laboratory results available within 35 days of onset, the timeliness of field activities (e.g., collecting two samples at least 24 hours apart within 11 days of paralysis onset), and the timeliness of notification (e.g., reporting AFP cases by sex within seven days of paralysis onset). Additionally, the number of healthcare encounters between onset and notification (≤2 encounters) is tracked by sex. The professional profile of staff, categorized by sex, is also monitored, including the proportion of women among surveillance officers, supervisors, and community-based surveillance informants. Furthermore, the number of surveillance staff trained in preventing and responding to sexual exploitation, abuse, and harassment (PRSEAH) is recorded. Environmental sample collection for poliovirus surveillance requires detailed documentation. This includes the name of the sample collector, location details (country, state, district, ward, and site identification), type of site (e.g., sewage plant or system), date and time of collection, and observations such as flow rate, adequacy of sample volume, and the presence of industrial effluents. Any issues during collection, such as delays due to rain or changes in sampling points, must be noted. The date the sample is sent to the laboratory, intermediary laboratory details, and the date of receipt and shipment to the processing laboratory are also recorded. Observations regarding storage requirements before shipment should be documented. Poliomyelitis laboratory results include the classification of specimens (e.g., wild poliovirus [WPV], vaccine-derived poliovirus [VDPV], Sabin-like, or non-polio enterovirus [NPEV]). The diagnosis and classification of cases are categorized based on laboratory findings, and follow-up stool testing for children is tracked. Immunoglobulin levels and vaccination history, including the number and type of inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) and oral polio vaccine (OPV) doses received, are recorded. The vaccination status of close family members and the date of the last OPV campaign in the community are also noted. Eligibility for antiviral polio treatment and compliance with treatment protocols are assessed. The document acknowledges contributions from various experts and organizations. It was developed under the guidance of the WHO South-East Asia Regional Office leadership, with coordination by Dr. Sunil Bahl and Dr. Sudhir Khanal. Technical content was updated by Dr. Lalit Kant, with input from participants of a regional workshop held in Dhaka in June 2022. This workshop included national EPI program managers, VPD surveillance officers, WHO country office staff, UNICEF representatives, and external collaborators. WHO headquarters staff, including Dr. Anindya Bose and Dr. Heidi Soeters, reviewed the draft and provided technical inputs. Contributions were also made by WHO-SEARO staff, UNICEF representatives (led by Christopher Gregory), and US CDC experts (Dr. Ahmed Kassem and Dr. Michelle Morales), who coordinated inputs from their respective teams.
